quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on the vocabulary of satins and sateens: single interlacings, the move number, satinette and the striped satin.

questions.q: In a satin, how often is each end down within one repeat?
questions.explain: A satin is warp-faced: each end is lifted on every pick except one, so it is down on only one pick of the repeat. 'Every pick but one' describes a sateen end.

questions.q: A sateen is best described as:
options: A twill with a long float
A warp-faced weave in which each end is down once per repeat
A plain weave with a move number
A weft-faced weave in which each end is up on only one pick
questions.explain: In a sateen each end is up on only one pick, so the weft covers the face. A weave in which each end is down once per repeat is a satin, the warp-faced opposite.

questions.q: What does the move number do?
options: Gives the number of ends per dent
Fixes how many ends the single interlacing moves along on each successive pick
Sets how many healds the weave needs
questions.explain: On each pick the interlacing is placed a fixed number of ends along from the previous one; that number is the move number, and it is chosen so that no two interlacings touch.

questions.q: A move number of 1 is allowed for a satin because it is the simplest step.
questions.explain: A move of 1 (or of repeat − 1) places each interlacing next to the previous one, so the single marks line up as a diagonal: the result is a twill, not a satin.

questions.q: Why are the single interlacings of a satin scattered so that no two touch?
options: So that the interlacings never show as a line and the face stays smooth and lustrous
To reduce the number of healds
questions.explain: Touching interlacings would join up into a visible diagonal or ridge. Scattering them hides the binding points under the floats, which is what gives satin its smooth, lustrous face.

questions.q: What is a 4-end satinette?
options: An irregular arrangement of single lifts used because 4 has no valid move number
questions.explain: Moves 2 (shares a factor with 4) and 1 or 3 (give a twill) are all ruled out, so no true 4-end satin exists; the satinette is an irregular arrangement of one lift per pick instead.

questions.q: Which end-use does the lecture attach to the 8-end 7/1 satin?
questions.explain: The 7/1 satin, with its long seven-pick floats, is the weave of damask and of satin stripes; denim is a 3/1 twill and towelling is honeycomb or terry.

questions.q: A true 6-end satin can be constructed with a regular move number.
questions.explain: Every candidate move for 6 either shares a factor with it (2, 3, 4) or gives a twill (1, 5), so only an irregular 6-end satin is possible.

questions.q: What does the notation 4/1 satin mean for one end?
options: The end is up for 4 picks and down for 1, so the weave is warp-faced on 5 ends
The end is down for 4 picks and up for 1
Four ends per dent, one pick per shed
questions.explain: As with twills the numbers are the up/down order of one end: 4 up, 1 down, repeat 5. 'Down for 4, up for 1' is the 1/4 sateen.

questions.q: In the striped satin drawing the satin stripe looks dark and the sateen stripe light, although both use the same yarns. Why?
options: The satin stripe has more picks
The warp is dark and the weft light: the satin stripe shows warp on the face, the sateen stripe shows weft
The dye takes differently on long floats
The sateen stripe is woven more loosely
questions.explain: Face colour follows whichever thread system is on top. The 4/1 satin stripe shows mostly warp (dark) and the 1/4 sateen stripe mostly weft (light), with no change of yarn.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The move-number rule, the valid moves for each repeat, float length and face proportion, and what changes as the repeat grows.

questions.q: Which condition must a satin move number satisfy?
options: It must share no factor with the repeat and must not be 1 or repeat − 1
It must be half the repeat
It must be an even number
It must be a factor of the repeat
questions.explain: A move sharing a factor with the repeat makes the interlacings coincide or line up, and 1 or repeat − 1 gives a twill. A factor or half the repeat is exactly what is forbidden.

questions.q: Which move numbers are possible for a 5-end satin?
questions.explain: 1 and 4 give twills; 2 and 3 share no factor with 5, so both are valid. The 4/1 satin and 1/4 sateen in the lecture use moves 3 and 2.

questions.q: Which move numbers are possible for an 8-end satin?
questions.explain: 2, 4 and 6 share the factor 2 with 8; 1 and 7 give twills. That leaves 3 and 5, as the lecture's table shows.

questions.q: Why is 4 not a valid move number for an 8-end satin?
options: Because it would give a twill
Because 4 shares a factor with 8, so the interlacings fall on the same ends every other pick instead of covering all eight
questions.explain: Stepping 4 on an 8-end repeat returns to the starting end after two picks, so only two ends ever interlace and the weave breaks down. A twill is what moves 1 and 7 give.

questions.q: Why is 7 not a valid move for an 8-end satin even though it shares no factor with 8?
options: Because it equals repeat − 1 and so produces a twill
questions.explain: A move of repeat − 1 is the same as a move of 1 in the other direction: the interlacings sit side by side and form a diagonal, i.e. a twill.

questions.q: On a 5-end repeat, move 2 and move 3 give satins whose faint diagonals lean in opposite directions.
questions.explain: Moving 3 ends to the right on a 5-end repeat is the same as moving 2 ends to the left, so the two satins are mirror images: the same weave with the direction reversed.

questions.q: As the satin repeat grows from 5 ends to 8 ends, what happens to the warp float?
options: It gets longer (4 to 7 picks), giving more lustre but a less firm cloth
It gets shorter and the cloth firmer
questions.explain: Each end interlaces once per repeat, so the float is repeat − 1 picks: 4 in a 4/1 satin, 7 in a 7/1 satin. Longer floats are more lustrous and less firm.

questions.q: What percentage of the face of a 4/1 satin is covered by warp?
questions.explain: Each end is up 4 picks out of 5: 4 ÷ 5 = 80 % warp on the face. 20 % is the 1/4 sateen and 75 % a 3/1 twill.

questions.q: Using the move-number rule, how many different move numbers are possible for a 7-end satin?
questions.explain: The candidates are 2 to 5 (1 and 6 are excluded as twills) and none of 2, 3, 4, 5 shares a factor with 7, so all four are valid: 2, 3, 4 and 5.

questions.q: How are the 4/1 satin and the 1/4 sateen related?
options: The sateen has a longer repeat
The sateen is the back of the satin: where the satin shows warp, the sateen shows weft
questions.explain: Turn a 4/1 satin over and each end is up once and down four times: a 1/4 sateen. Both repeat on 5 ends and use 5 healds.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting filled squares, face proportions, floats, healds and interlacing positions on the point-paper repeats of the lecture.

questions.q: How many squares are filled in one 5 × 5 repeat of a 4/1 satin?
questions.explain: Each of the 5 ends is up on 4 picks: 5 × 4 = 20 filled squares out of 25, leaving 5 single interlacings.

questions.q: What percentage of the face of a 7/1 satin is warp? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: Each end is up 7 picks in 8: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875, i.e. 87.5 % warp on the face.

questions.q: How many squares are filled in one 8 × 8 repeat of a 1/7 sateen?
questions.explain: In a sateen each end is up on only one pick: 8 ends × 1 = 8 filled squares out of 64.

questions.q: A 5-end sateen uses move 2. Pick 1 lifts end 1. Which end is lifted on pick 4?
questions.explain: Add the move for each pick: pick 2 lifts end 3, pick 3 lifts end 5, pick 4 lifts end 7 − 5 = end 2. The sequence 1, 3, 5, 2, 4 visits every end once.

questions.q: An 8-end satin uses move 3. The single interlacing on pick 1 is on end 1. On which end is the interlacing on pick 3?
questions.explain: Pick 2: end 1 + 3 = 4; pick 3: 4 + 3 = 7. No wrap-round is needed until pick 4 (10 − 8 = end 2).

questions.q: How many heald frames does an 8-end 7/1 satin need with a straight draft?
questions.explain: Each of the 8 ends in the repeat interlaces on a different pick, so no two ends move alike: 8 frames, the limit of a tappet loom.

questions.q: How many picks long is the longest warp float in a 4/1 satin?
questions.explain: An end that is down on only one pick of 5 floats over the other 4: float = repeat − 1 = 4 picks.

questions.q: The striped satin is drawn on 10 ends × 10 picks: five ends of 4/1 satin beside five ends of 1/4 sateen. How many squares are filled?
questions.explain: Satin stripe: 5 ends up on 8 of the 10 picks = 40. Sateen stripe: 5 ends up on 2 of 10 picks = 10. Total 50 of 100.

questions.q: The 4-end satinette is written $8 $4 $1 $2 −4, first code at the bottom. Which end is lifted on pick 3?
questions.explain: $1 is 0001 with the most significant bit on the left end, so the lift is on end 4. Picks 1 to 4 lift ends 1, 2, 4, 3: one lift per pick, in broken-twill order.

questions.q: A 10-end satin uses move 3; the interlacing on pick 1 is on end 1. On which end is it on pick 5?
questions.explain: Four moves of 3 from end 1 give 1 + 12 = 13; subtracting the 10-end repeat leaves end 3. Forgetting to wrap round gives the impossible 'end 13'.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Choosing satins and sateens for real orders and spotting what has gone wrong on the design table or the loom.

questions.q: A buyer wants a smooth, highly lustrous warp-faced furnishing fabric. Which weave do you propose?
questions.explain: The 7/1 satin has the longest floats and the most warp on the face, giving maximum lustre. A 1/4 sateen puts weft on the face and the satinette is only a broken twill.

questions.q: A trainee draws an 8-end 'satin' with move 2. What will the drawing show?
options: A sateen instead of a satin
The interlacings fall on only four ends and line up, because 2 shares a factor with 8
questions.explain: Stepping 2 on 8 ends returns to end 1 after four picks, so ends 3, 5, 7 never interlace and the marks stack in columns. A valid move must be 3 or 5.

questions.q: A tappet loom in the mill has only 4 heald frames and a customer wants a satin-like cloth. What can you offer?
options: A 4-end satinette, the irregular one-lift-per-pick arrangement
A 5-end satin with two ends per heald
questions.explain: No true 4-end satin exists, and a 5-end satin needs 5 healds. The 4-end satinette ($8 $4 $1 $2) runs on 4 frames and gives a broken 1/3 twill that reads as a small satin.

questions.q: A striped satin is woven with dark warp and light weft. The customer wants one more stripe to look light. What do you change?
options: Weave that stripe as 1/4 sateen so the weft shows on the face
questions.explain: Face colour follows the thread on top. Switching the stripe to sateen puts the light weft on the face, exactly as in the lecture's striped satin, without any change of yarn.

questions.q: A sample of 4/1 satin arrives for inspection and the surface shows mostly weft. The most likely explanation is:
options: The inspector is looking at the back, which is a 1/4 sateen
questions.explain: The back of a 4/1 satin is a 1/4 sateen with 80 % weft on it. Turn the sample over before raising a complaint.

questions.q: Why does an 8-end satin snag more easily than a 2/2 twill of the same yarns?
options: Because it uses a move number
Because its warp floats over 7 picks instead of 2, so a loose float is easily caught
questions.explain: Snagging risk rises with float length. The 7/1 satin's floats are more than three times as long as a 2/2 twill's, which is the price of its lustre.

questions.q: Why is the 8-end satin the weave chosen for damask table linen?
options: Because its floats are very short
Because it needs fewer healds than a 5-end satin
Because the figure is formed by exchanging 7/1 satin and 1/7 sateen areas, whose long floats contrast strongly in lustre
Because it is cheaper to weave than plain weave
questions.explain: Damask shows its pattern through the contrast between warp-faced and weft-faced satin areas, and the long 7-pick floats give the strongest lustre difference.

questions.q: With the same yarn, a satin can be set more densely than a plain weave.
questions.explain: A satin end interlaces only once per repeat, so there is far less yarn crowding at crossings than in plain weave and the threads can be packed closer.

questions.q: Two designers propose a 5-end satin, one with move 2 and one with move 3. What is the practical difference?
options: Only the direction of the faint diagonal; the float length and face proportion are the same
questions.explain: Both give an 80 % warp face, 4-pick floats and a 5-end repeat; they are mirror images. The choice usually follows the yarn twist so the diagonal is hidden.

questions.q: Can a 1/4 sateen be woven on a tappet loom with 6 heald frames?
options: Yes: it repeats on 5 ends and 5 picks, so 5 frames and a 5-pick tappet suffice
questions.explain: The 5-end sateen has five different end movements and a 5-pick repeat, well within a tappet's 6 to 8 frames and 8-pick limit.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across the lecture: testing move numbers, reading hex, two-step face-proportion reasoning and the slips students make most.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid move number for a 10-end satin?
questions.explain: 2 and 5 share factors with 10 and 9 is repeat − 1 (a twill). The valid moves are 3 and 7, as the lecture's table gives.

questions.q: Apply the move-number rule to a 9-end satin. How many valid move numbers are there?
questions.explain: Candidates run from 2 to 7 (six numbers); 3 and 6 share the factor 3 with 9 and are struck out, leaving 2, 4, 5 and 7: four valid moves.

questions.q: A student claims a 7-end satin is impossible because 7 is a prime number. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: prime repeats cannot form satins
A prime repeat shares no factor with any smaller number, so every move from 2 to 5 is valid
Only even repeats can be satins
questions.explain: Sharing no factor is the condition for a valid move, so a prime repeat has the most choices: 2, 3, 4 and 5. Only 1 and 6 are excluded as twills.

questions.q: Compared with a 5-end 4/1 satin, which statement about the 8-end 7/1 satin is FALSE?
options: Its face carries a higher proportion of warp
questions.explain: The 7/1 satin needs 8 frames against 5. Floats (7 against 4), warp proportion (87.5 % against 80 %) and repeat (8 against 5) are all larger.

questions.q: What percentage of the face of a 1/7 sateen is weft? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: Each end is up only 1 pick in 8, so weft shows on 7 ÷ 8 = 87.5 % of the face: the mirror of the 7/1 satin.

questions.q: The lifts of the 4-end satinette form a broken 1/3 twill.
questions.explain: One lift per pick on ends 1, 2, 4, 3 is a 1/3 twill whose order is broken after the second pick, which hides the diagonal.

questions.q: Decode $8 $4 $1 $2 −4 (first code = bottom pick). On picks 1 to 4 the lifted ends are:
questions.explain: $8 = 1000 (end 1), $4 = 0100 (end 2), $1 = 0001 (end 4), $2 = 0010 (end 3). Reading the bits as end 4 first gives the reversed sequence, a common slip.

questions.q: What percentage of the BACK of a 4/1 satin is covered by warp?
questions.explain: The face is 80 % warp, so the back shows warp only where the end is down: 1 pick in 5, i.e. 20 %. The back of a satin is a sateen.

questions.q: The striped satin is drawn on 10 ends × 10 picks, yet each stripe weave repeats on 5 picks. What is the true repeat of the design?
questions.explain: The width must include both 5-end stripes (10 ends), but both satin and sateen repeat on 5 picks; the 10-pick drawing simply shows two repeats.

questions.q: An 8-end satin uses move 5 and the interlacing on pick 1 is on end 1. On which end is the interlacing on pick 3?
questions.explain: Pick 2: 1 + 5 = end 6; pick 3: 6 + 5 = 11, minus the 8-end repeat = end 3. Move 5 is move 3 in the other direction.
